subject: BRGSA
subjectTitle: Business Research and Growth Systems Architecture

sections.rule: One correct option. Two marks each. No negative marking.
A short scenario, then a task. Both parts must be right for the marks. No partial credit.
A complete structured response. Not machine-marked.

paper.stem: A useful pricing change genuinely improves conversion, but an underpowered test concludes that nothing changed. Which error is this?
options: A Type I error, a false positive
No error because the result was not significant
Survivorship bias alone, with no testing error involved
A Type II error, a false negative

paper.caselet: Two landing pages report the same 8% signup rate. Page A was shown to the stated ICP through targeted traffic. Page B was sent to friends, employees, and a prize-seeking giveaway list.
paper.stem: Which conclusion is defensible?
options: Both pages prove exactly equal demand because the measured conversion rate is identical
Neither page can ever be used for validation because landing pages are not real products
Page B carries the stronger signal because its audience was larger
Page A carries the more trustworthy demand signal because the traffic matches the intended market

paper.caselet: Traffic is healthy, signup conversion is healthy, but only 12% of new accounts complete the first value event. The team proposes buying more ads.
paper.stem: What should the growth diagnosis prioritize?
options: Activation—the narrowest current constraint
A lower sample-size target
A full company rebrand exercise
More top-of-funnel traffic volume

paper.caselet: Variant B leads after 18 visitors per arm. The pre-set sample target is 1,000 per arm.
paper.stem: What is the sound next action?
options: Stop the test and ship Variant B before the current lead disappears
Run the test to completion at the pre-calculated sample size
Delete Variant A from the final written report
Double-count repeat visitors to finish sooner

paper.caselet: A D2C brand validates demand with paid pre-orders. Its first cohort activates through a 21-day routine, repurchase predicts retention, and acquisition is profitable. The team now has ten experiment ideas but capacity for two.
paper.stem: Which sequence best protects the evidence chain?
options: Choose the two ideas with the highest reach scores and run them
Name the current constraint, score ideas against it with evidence/capacity, pre-register decisions, then reallocate after results
Run all ten with smaller samples each
Optimise for the total follower count across all channels instead

paper.stem: Why must a B2B pipeline define entry and exit criteria for each stage?
options: To increase the number of email opens recorded across each outreach sequence sent to the list
To make the CRM records look complete and tidy for internal reporting purposes each quarter
So conversion always reflects real buyer progress and never a subjective sales label
To avoid having to speak to customers directly at any point in the process

paper.caselet: A SaaS company grows 35% through new sales, but the starting cohort falls from ₹20 lakh to ₹16 lakh MRR after expansion, churn, and downgrades.
paper.stem: What does the cohort's NRR say?
options: NRR is 80%; acquisition is masking a shrinking base
NRR cannot be calculated without new sales figures
NRR is 35% for this cohort
NRR is 125%, so the revenue base is compounding

paper.caselet: A product has a small but stable retention plateau and acceptable unit economics among one narrow segment. Its broad campaign performs poorly.
paper.stem: Which decision is best supported?
options: Scale the broad acquisition campaign immediately across every channel
Pivot away from the product entirely without doing any segment analysis first
Ignore retention altogether and optimise for total impressions delivered instead
Always iterate around the retained segment before considering a full pivot

paper.stem: What makes lean validation different from simply doing more market research?
options: It always turns the demand assumption into a test whose threshold is set before any build
It replaces customer evidence with the founder's own judgment about the problem
It estimates the total addressable market from desk research before speaking to any real buyers
It begins only after the product is complete and ready to put in front of customers

paper.caselet: Two companies each average $10,000 in annual revenue per account. One charges a flat rate; the other charges per seat. A year later the second has grown revenue per account substantially and the first has not, with no change in either customer base.
paper.stem: What explains the difference?
options: The per-seat company raised its list price during the year, which the flat-rate company chose not to do.
The structures make different promises about growth: per-seat revenue grows as a customer's team grows, flat rate does not.
The per-seat company's customers were larger organisations to begin with, so the same structure produced more revenue from each of them.
The flat-rate company has better retention, which it bought by holding its price steady through the year.

paper.caselet: A fitness app gives ₹100 for each invite. Invites spike, but the product is no more useful to existing users when friends join, and the spike ends when the reward stops.
paper.stem: What was built?
options: A durable and defensible network effect between the users
An incentivised referral campaign, not a network effect
A habit loop, by the course's own working definition
A pricing-led revenue expansion engine for the existing base

paper.stem: Why estimate LTV before 18 months of mature data exists?
options: To claim a precise figure for future revenue in the plan
To replace retention measurement altogether with a single summary number that is easier to report
Because CAC never carries decision meaning without an estimate of the value it buys
Because all customers turn out to have roughly the same lifetime value anyway in practice

paper.stem: Which pair most directly separates ‘how much revenue left’ from ‘when customer groups disengage’?
options: Email sends and open rate
CAC and total ad reach
Total customer count and impressions
Gross revenue churn and cohort/time-to-churn analysis

paper.caselet: Onboarding asks a new user a multiple-choice preference question before they can proceed. The product team argues it is helpful because it personalises the experience.
paper.stem: How should the step be judged?
options: Replace it with a smart default unless the answer is required to reach the aha, since only that justifies a step.
Keep it but move it later in the flow, which preserves the personalisation while reducing the number of early steps.
Keep it, since personalisation raises long-term retention and the cost of answering one question is small against that eventual gain.
Remove it and every other optional step, because onboarding should contain nothing but the single shortest path.

paper.stem: Which view best helps locate when and for whom churn occurs?
options: Cohort retention and time-to-churn together, always segmented by the relevant customer unit
The total number of emails ever sent
The all-time cumulative count of customers acquired
The total quarterly advertising impressions delivered across all channels

paper.caselet: A team spends ₹2,00,000 on a paid channel. Their average contract value is ₹1,000 a month and their acquisition cost on that channel lands near ₹8,000.
paper.stem: What should the team do?
options: Stop the channel on price-point mismatch, because that arithmetic is settled before any creative decision is taken.
Keep the channel and raise the price, since a contract worth more would make the same acquisition cost acceptable.
Improve the creative and the targeting first, since a high acquisition cost usually reflects a weak campaign rather than the channel.
Continue for a full quarter, because paid channels need time before their true cost per customer can be judged.

paper.caselet: A team wants to test whether a new call-to-action improves signups. One member proposes stating the hypothesis as "the new wording feels more natural to users".
paper.stem: What is wrong with that as a hypothesis?
options: It should predict a larger effect, because a small improvement is not worth the cost of running a test at all.
It is not falsifiable: every experiment starts from a stated no-difference position that a specific, measurable claim can argue against.
It fails to say which variant is the control, without which the two groups cannot be compared.
It names the wrong metric, since signups are what the team cares about rather than how the wording feels.

paper.caselet: Seven onboarding steps each lose only a small percentage of users, but fewer than one-third reach the first value event.
paper.stem: Which principle best explains the result?
options: The aha moment must always be the signup event itself by definition
Adding more explanatory steps will always fix the cognitive load problem
Small step-level losses at each stage cannot compound into anything
Reasonable step-level friction always compounds across the whole path to aha

paper.stem: Why does the course place habit loops beneath retention, referral, and lifecycle work?
options: Because a habit eliminates the need for the product to deliver any value at all
Because a repeatable cue-action-reward cycle makes return behaviour recur without ever reacquiring the user
Because every product should be sending daily notifications to its users
Because habit formation is really just another kind of pricing model

paper.caselet: A founder has budgeted six months to build an AI meeting recorder and a marketing campaign to launch it. A colleague suggests putting up a page with the real offer and seeing whether anyone acts on it, before any of that starts.
paper.stem: What is the strongest argument for running the page first?
options: Building first is the more reliable route to learning, because real usage data from a working product is stronger evidence than a page view.
The page removes the risk from the build, since a positive result means the product can be scoped with confidence.
Every plan that goes straight to build carries an untested demand assumption, and the test buys that certainty in days rather than months.
A landing page produces marketing material the launch campaign is going to need anyway, so none of the work is wasted either way.

paper.caselet: A dashboard celebrates visits and downloads every week, but no number has an owner, a threshold, or a stated action for when it moves.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Ship the change if the founder likes the way the chart looks at the end. (Decision rules)
If the result looks promising once it lands, then the team will sit down and discuss scaling it up. (Decision rules)
Pre-register the decision each metric will trigger before the result arrives, so a movement in the number changes an action rather than a narrative. (Decision rules)
Choose the decision threshold only after seeing how the control group actually performed during the whole test period. (Decision rules)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Decision rules: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.
Decision rules: A metric earns a place on the dashboard only when it carries an owner, a threshold, and an action already agreed for the moment it crosses that threshold.

Decision rules: ICE scores each idea on impact against the current constraint, confidence backed by evidence that can be named, and ease including the time to a credible signal, turning a list of ideas into an ordered backlog.
Decision rules: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.

paper.caselet: A channel reaches the intended buyer precisely but takes fourteen months to produce revenue, and the company has three months of runway.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: The product clearly cannot have found product-market fit yet. (Channel fit)
All B2B products require television advertising in order to reach the relevant decision-makers at scale. (Channel fit)
The high view count is proof enough that the channel is working exactly as intended. (Channel fit)
Score candidate channels against the product's economics and timing constraints before spending, and reject one that fails any single dimension. (Channel fit)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Channel fit: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.
Channel fit: Activation is the first observable moment a user experiences the promised value, and every step standing between signup and that moment sheds a share of the users still remaining.
Channel fit: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.

Channel fit: Every channel has fixed properties — targeting, control, input cost, output quality, time to result and economics — and it fits only when those match the product's buyer and unit economics.

paper.caselet: One segment returns close to five times its acquisition cost and another barely one, yet the team spends equally on both because the blended figure looks acceptable.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Pivot away from the product entirely without doing any segment analysis first. (CAC and LTV)
Apply the joining test — does one more user make the product more valuable to existing users — and run the referral playbook when the answer is no. (CAC and LTV)
Estimate LTV from the cohort behaviour already visible, compare it with CAC segment by segment, and let that ratio decide which segment to acquire more of. (CAC and LTV)
Ignore retention altogether and optimise for total impressions delivered instead. (CAC and LTV)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: CAC and LTV: A cohort groups users by when they entered so retention can be compared at equal age, which aggregate totals cannot do because they mix new arrivals with survivors.
CAC and LTV: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.
CAC and LTV: CAC carries no decision meaning without an estimate of the value it buys, so LTV is estimated early from observed lifespan, margin and revenue rather than waited for.

CAC and LTV: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.

paper.caselet: A high-visibility feature scores well on team enthusiasm, has no evidence behind its confidence score, needs a quarter of engineering, and does not touch the activation step the funnel math identified.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Apply the joining test — does one more user make the product more valuable to existing users — and run the referral playbook when the answer is no. (Prioritisation)
Score every candidate experiment against the current primary constraint, and cap confidence at five whenever the supporting evidence cannot be named in one sentence. (Prioritisation)
Add another forty ideas to the existing backlog list. (Prioritisation)
Run every test in parallel at the same time. (Prioritisation)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Prioritisation: A metric earns a place on the dashboard only when it carries an owner, a threshold, and an action already agreed for the moment it crosses that threshold.
Prioritisation: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.

Prioritisation: ICE scores each idea on impact against the current constraint, confidence backed by evidence that can be named, and ease including the time to a credible signal, turning a list of ideas into an ordered backlog.

Prioritisation: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.
